learningObjective: Recognise the scope limits and common overclaims around single-paper quantization results (SmoothQuant, GPTQ, AWQ).

canonicalClaims.claim: Quantization papers such as SmoothQuant, GPTQ and AWQ report accuracy and speedup on specific model families, specific bit widths, specific calibration sets and specific hardware/kernels; treating any of these results as universal LLM properties (across model families, sizes, tasks, or hardware) overgeneralizes their conclusions.
conditions: The paper's evaluation defines the model families, tasks, and calibration corpora.
The kernel/hardware combination is stated explicitly.
nonImplications: Does not imply the techniques never generalize; empirically they often do, but each application must be re-evaluated.
Does not imply the papers' comparisons among themselves are invalid within their own reported settings.

canonicalClaims.claim: Reported end-to-end speedup from a quantization paper depends on the availability of an efficient dequantized-GEMM kernel for the target precision/granularity on the target hardware; the same quantization scheme can be faster on one GPU generation and no faster (or slower) on another due to Tensor Core precision support and library kernels.
conditions: The claim is about wall-clock speedup, not model size.
nonImplications: Does not imply memory footprint reduction from quantization is hardware-dependent; footprint reduction is largely arithmetic and hardware-independent.

canonicalClaims.claim: An ablation supports only the specific factor it isolates; e.g. SmoothQuant's ablation of the migration factor α supports that α trades off activation vs weight quantization difficulty, but does not by itself establish that SmoothQuant is superior to GPTQ or AWQ at every setting.
conditions: The ablation isolates the intended variable.
nonImplications: Does not imply ablations are irrelevant to cross-paper comparisons; they inform mechanism, not head-to-head verdicts.

misconceptions.claim: Because SmoothQuant, GPTQ and AWQ all report high accuracy at 4-bit/8-bit, one can conclude that 'LLMs are always safe to quantize to 4 bits with negligible accuracy loss'.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Papers report on specific model families, sizes and tasks. Long-tail tasks, smaller models, math and code tasks often suffer more; the universal claim exceeds the evidence.

misconceptions.claim: A quantization paper's reported speedup is a property of the bit width alone and is independent of hardware and available kernels.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Speedup depends on kernel availability for the specific precision/granularity on the target hardware; without an efficient dequant-GEMM, memory savings do not translate to latency savings.

misconceptions.claim: An ablation study of a single hyperparameter in a paper establishes that the paper's method is superior to all competing methods at all settings.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Ablations isolate a mechanism; they do not perform head-to-head comparison against other papers' methods.
